name: Cyproheptadine
lead: Cyproheptadine is a first-generation antihistamine that also blocks serotonin 5-HT2 receptors and has anticholinergic and sedating effects. It is approved for allergic conditions such as seasonal and perennial rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis and urticaria.[2][3] Increased appetite and weight gain are recognised effects of the drug, and it is prescribed off-label as an appetite stimulant, particularly in children with poor weight gain, cystic fibrosis or failure to thrive.[3][4]

In appearance communities it is discussed as a weight-gain aid for people who struggle to eat enough to build size, a category the wiki files under muscle. The link to looks is indirect: a larger appetite can mean more calories eaten, which can support a bulk with resistance training. A T Nation forum contributor in 2007 listed it among appetite aids and described it as raising appetite and growth hormone secretion.[13]

Published human work on its appetite effect is mostly in medical populations: a randomised trial in anorexia nervosa in the 1970s, retrospective and small controlled studies in children with cystic fibrosis or failure to thrive, and registered trials in children with cancer-related weight loss.[5][6][7][14][15][16] No published trial has tested it for cosmetic or bodybuilding goals in healthy adults.

Reported adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and urinary retention, and, rarely, liver injury and blood disorders. The US label warns about overdose in children.[2][3]

paras: The US label lists perennial and seasonal allergic rhinitis, vasomotor rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, mild urticaria and angioedema, cold urticaria, dermatographism, and adjunctive therapy in anaphylaxis.[2] In the UK and some other countries it is also labelled for migraine prevention.[3] Wikipedia notes that second-generation antihistamines such as loratadine and ketotifen have shown similar results in allergy with fewer side effects.[3]

Off-label uses described in reference sources include serotonin syndrome, insomnia, antipsychotic-induced akathisia, cyclical vomiting in infants and some skin conditions; a 2024 network meta-analysis in JAMA Network Open compared drugs for antipsychotic-induced akathisia.[3][17]

Weight gain observed in patients during allergy treatment led to its off-label use in underweight children, including those with cystic fibrosis or failure to thrive.[3][4] Grokipedia dates the noticing of the appetite effect to the mid-1960s and says the proposed mechanism is blockade of 5-HT2 receptors in the hypothalamus, which it presents as likely rather than established; Wikipedia attributes the effect to antiserotonergic action.[3][4] Wikipedia's article on appetite stimulants lists cyproheptadine with megestrol, dronabinol and mirtazapine as drugs used for appetite loss or muscle wasting linked to conditions such as cystic fibrosis, cancer and AIDS, and says no drug apart from dronabinol for HIV-related anorexia has FDA approval specifically for appetite.[18]
In Turkey, Grokipedia says, cyproheptadine is available only by prescription and is the main drug used for weight gain.[4]

Cyproheptadine is a potent H1 receptor antagonist and also strongly blocks 5-HT2 receptors, with anticholinergic, antidopaminergic and local anesthetic activity; it crosses the blood-brain barrier.[3] PET imaging reported by Wikipedia showed about 85 percent 5-HT2 blockade at one therapeutic regimen and 95 percent at a higher one.[3] It is well absorbed orally, peaks after about 1 to 4 hours, is highly protein bound (96 to 99 percent), and is mainly metabolised in the liver and excreted in urine and faeces.[3]

The 5-HT2A antagonism led to its study as a so-called trip killer for serotonergic psychedelics, with inconclusive results; a 2026 review in the Journal of Psychopharmacology says no systematic evaluation of such agents exists.[3][16] Studies of serotonin in locomotion and spinal injury cite cyproheptadine as a serotonin-receptor antagonist tool in laboratory work.[8][9]
It is also used in veterinary medicine as an appetite stimulant in cats and as a second-line treatment for pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction in horses.[3]

Cyproheptadine was patented in 1959 and introduced for medical use in 1961.[3] Grokipedia says it was developed by Merck & Co., that the US patent was filed on 29 September 1958 and issued on 26 December 1961, and that the FDA approved it on 17 October 1961 as Periactin; Wikipedia does not name the developer.[3][4] Use as an appetite stimulant followed early observations of weight gain in pediatric allergy patients.[4]

It is sold worldwide, including in Australia, Canada, Europe, India, Japan, Mexico, the UK and the US, and in 2023 it was the 234th most prescribed medication in the US with more than one million prescriptions.[3]

Looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums mention cyproheptadine mainly as one appetite-raising option among several. A post in a 2007 T Nation thread says that clinical appetite stimulants megestrol acetate and dronabinol are used in AIDS, burn and cancer patients and cause mostly fat gain, while cyproheptadine is an antihistamine and serotonin antagonist that increases growth hormone secretion and appetite.[13] A looksmax.org thread reposts a post from the Ray Peat-inspired supplement community in which a writer, Haidut, recommends a combination of pregnenolone, clonidine and cyproheptadine for stress and low motivation.[1]

The Peat-inspired post that opens the looksmax.org thread discusses acidifying foods and growth hormone, saying Ray Peat regards high growth hormone as associated with disease; the same post recommends cyproheptadine, and the thread does not address how this squares with reports of a growth-hormone effect.[1]

Common effects are sedation (often transient), dizziness, confusion and restlessness, along with anticholinergic effects including blurred vision, constipation, dry mouth, urinary retention and fast heart rate; increased appetite and weight gain are also listed.[2][3] Rare serious effects include convulsions, hallucinations, hypotension, anaphylaxis, hemolytic anemia, blood disorders and liver injury including hepatitis and liver failure.[3] The label warns that antihistamine overdose in infants and children may cause hallucinations, central nervous system depression, convulsions and death, and that effects add to those of alcohol and other sedatives.[2]

Contraindications listed in reference material include newborns and premature infants, nursing mothers, narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention, symptomatic prostatic hypertrophy and concurrent monoamine oxidase inhibitor use.[3][4] A 2025 retrospective study of 119 children with cyclic vomiting syndrome reported that 6 of the 66 given cyproheptadine stopped it because of drowsiness or weight gain.[16] The label places the drug in pregnancy category B.[2]

Wikipedia lists cyproheptadine as prescription-only in the United States and Canada, general sales (over the counter) in the United Kingdom, and pharmacist-only (Schedule 3) in Australia, noting that its infobox also lists it as generally over the counter, which conflicts with the country entries.[3] It is not described as a controlled substance.
No studies have tested cyproheptadine for cosmetic weight gain or muscle building in healthy people.

In 1979, Goldberg, Halmi, Eckert, Casper and Davis reported in the British Journal of Psychiatry a trial of 81 women with anorexia nervosa from three hospitals, randomly assigned to cyproheptadine or placebo with or without behaviour therapy. Cyproheptadine helped a subgroup gain weight: those with a history of delivery complications, who had lost 41 to 52 percent of normal weight and had failed outpatient treatment.[14]

In cystic fibrosis, a 2023 retrospective study of 62 children taking cyproheptadine or mirtazapine for at least six months found a weight z-score increase at three months (adjusted mean difference 0.33), with improved lung function at three and six months, and a 2025 retrospective study of 45 children found significant weight and BMI z-score improvement by three months with smaller gains from three to six months.[15] Grokipedia summarises a 12-week randomised trial in children and adolescents with cystic fibrosis reporting mean weight gain of 3.45 kg versus 1.1 kg with placebo, and a systematic review of 46 studies in which 85 percent showed significant weight gain, while noting it does not describe the methods of the latter.[4]

A 2026 non-randomised study in Frontiers in Pharmacology compared 25 children aged 1 to 3 with failure to thrive and food allergy given cyproheptadine for 12 weeks against 19 untreated controls; treated children had higher body weight (10.32 versus 9.05 kg) and larger improvements in weight and BMI z-scores, with no difference in height.[16]

Registered clinical trials examine it in other medical contexts: a completed phase 2 trial of cyproheptadine and megestrol to prevent weight loss in 70 children with cancer cachexia,[5] two terminated pediatric cancer trials of weight loss prevention,[6][10] a terminated trial in pediatric feeding disorders,[7] and COVID-19 and ADHD trials unrelated to appetite.[11][12] Results of these registrations are not summarised in the registry entries cited here.

lore.intro: Cyproheptadine is mentioned only occasionally in these communities, in bodybuilding discussion of appetite aids and in Ray Peat-inspired supplement circles rather than as a dedicated weight-gain protocol.[1][13]

claims.claim: Cyproheptadine, combined with pregnenolone and clonidine, lowers stress and addresses ADD.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread reposts a post by a Peat-community writer recommending a combination of pregnenolone, clonidine and cyproheptadine for stress and low motivation, arguing the immediate problems should be addressed first.[1]
claims.experts: The US label lists only allergic indications for cyproheptadine.[2] No published trial of this combination for stress or attention problems is cited in the label or reference summaries reviewed.[3]

claims.claim: Cyproheptadine is a useful appetite stimulant for gaining weight.
claims.believers: Off-label prescribers and patient communities describe using it for poor appetite, particularly in underweight children.[4]
claims.experts: Increased appetite and weight gain are recognised effects, and studies in children with cystic fibrosis, failure to thrive and anorexia nervosa report weight gain, but use in healthy adults for cosmetic purposes has not been studied.[3][14][15][16]

claims.claim: It increases growth hormone and helps build muscle.
claims.believers: A T Nation contributor describes it as an antihistamine and serotonin antagonist that increases growth hormone secretion and appetite, as an alternative to appetite drugs that mostly add fat.[13]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested cyproheptadine for muscle gain in healthy people, and the references reviewed attribute its weight effect to appetite through serotonin blockade.[3][4]

claims.claim: Growth hormone is harmful and acidifying foods lower it.
claims.believers: The Peat-community post that opens a looksmax.org thread says Ray Peat treats high growth hormone as associated with disease and describes lowering plasma pH as inhibiting its release.[1]
claims.experts: No study tests this claim in connection with cyproheptadine.

claims.claim: It is safe because it is an old, widely prescribed allergy drug.
claims.believers: Users point to its long history and wide availability, including over the counter in the UK.[3]
claims.experts: The label lists sedation and anticholinergic effects, rare liver and blood disorders, and overdose dangers in children.[2][3]

card.summary: An allergy antihistamine prescribed off-label for appetite in children; never tested for cosmetic weight gain.
card.note: Sedating and anticholinergic; overdose is dangerous in children. Rx in US and Canada, OTC in the UK.

quick.overview:
Cyproheptadine is an older antihistamine approved for allergies. Because it also blocks serotonin receptors, it increases appetite, and doctors sometimes prescribe it off-label to underweight children.

In appearance forums it comes up as a weight-gain aid and in supplement-stack discussions. No trial has tested it in healthy adults for cosmetic purposes.
quick.mechanism: It blocks histamine H1 and serotonin 5-HT2 receptors and also has anticholinergic and sedating effects. Its appetite effect is attributed to blocking serotonin signalling, though the mechanism is not fully settled.
quick.risks: Common effects are drowsiness, dizziness and dry mouth. Rare liver and blood problems are reported, and overdose in children can cause convulsions and death. It is prescription-only in the US and Canada and over the counter in the UK.
